gap: No result ChatGPT got states how bright each pick is on the screen size the answer recommends. On a 120-inch, gain-1.0 screen, ProjectorCentral's measured lumens give the Nebula X1 60.6 ft-L in Standard mode. The Mars 3 gets 16.1 ft-L in Movie mode, which just meets the SMPTE dark-room target, and only about 6 ft-L in the Eco mode that its 5-hour battery claim relies on. So the Mars 3 is a 120-inch-or-smaller projector for after dark, not a 120–150-inch one.
standout_why: Pages compared: Wirecutter (proxy copy) gives Mars 3 lumens (over 800 max, over 600 Custom) and runtimes (about 2 h at 100%, 4 h 45 min in eco) but no foot-lamberts or nits at any screen size. ProjectorCentral's X1 review lists per-mode lumens but no ft-L and no screen-size advice. ProjectorCentral's Mars 3 review lists per-mode and eco lumens but no ft-L. The RTINGS outdoor, X1 and Horizon 20 pages came back as navigation only through the fetch tool, and Yahoo Tech returned 403, so neither was checked for ft-L. None of the pages I could read turns lumens into on-screen brightness at 120 or 150 inches, or gives the largest screen each pick can light to 16 ft-L.
decides: This supports the X1 as the bright-backyard pick: 60.6 ft-L at 120 inches and 38.8 ft-L at 150 inches in Standard mode, with 16 ft-L reachable up to about a 233-inch image. It narrows the Mars 3 recommendation. ChatGPT pitched the 120–150-inch screen size in the same answer, but in Movie mode the Mars 3 reaches 16 ft-L only up to about 120 inches (142 inches in Bright mode). On the eco setting behind the long runtime, the 16 ft-L limit drops to about 74–97 inches. On a full-brightness charge (about 2 h per Wirecutter) you get one feature-length film. The Horizon 20, at 39.4 ft-L at 120 inches in Movie mode on the maker's $1,559 price, is the cheapest measured candidate per lumen and can still light about 188 inches to 16 ft-L.

findings.label: Foot-lambert formula and targets
findings.value: ft-L = lumens × gain ÷ screen ft²; SMPTE target 16 ft-L (allowed range 12–22); family room with some light about 50 ft-L
findings.source_title: Simple Guide to Calculating Projector Lumens (M. David Stone, ProjectorCentral, 2019-10-11)
findings.note: All figures below assume a gain-1.0 screen. 120-inch 16:9 = 104.59 × 58.83 in = 42.73 ft²; 150-inch = 66.76 ft²; 16:9 area in ft² = diag² × 0.4273 ÷ 144.

unsourced: Cosmos 4K SE measured lumens: search snippets cite CNET (Geoffrey Morrison) measuring 1,219 lm. cnet.com was blocked to the fetch tool and the mirror returned 410. TechRadar and Digital Camera World returned only page titles. ProjectorCentral has a spec page but I found no SE lab review.
Nebula X1 measured power draw in watts, which I needed for hours on a power station: not in ProjectorCentral's review. The maker's 3.32 h figure on an Anker SOLIX C1000 is for the X1 Pro, not the X1.
Horizon 20 measured lumens from RTINGS: the RTINGS review and the outdoor best-list page returned only navigation through the fetch tool, and the curl download was not permitted.
Inverter or conversion efficiency for running AC projectors from a power station: no sourced figure, so power-station hours above are upper bounds.
Prices behind ChatGPT's cards ($1,899 X1, $899.99 Mars 3, $989.99 Cosmos 4K SE): the retailer was not named, so I did not check them. Maker US store prices are used instead.
Yahoo Tech and Forbes rival pages: Yahoo returned 403; I did not open Forbes, so I could not confirm whether they give foot-lamberts.
